title: 30-Year Mystery Solved: 400 Gold Coins Found at Sea Belonged to Dutch Ship
summary:
In 1995, divers exploring the seafloor off the coast of Devon, England, made a stunning discovery: more than 400 gold coins glinting in the sand at a depth of 60 feet, alongside gold jewelry, a pure gold nugget, and a fish-shaped sounding weight. The treasure clearly came from a shipwreck, but its origin remained a mystery for three decades.

Key clues included a pewter bowl and spoon of Dutch origin, which narrowed the search. Historian Ian Friel unearthed archival documents that finally cracked the case. The ship was identified as the Dom van Keulen, a Dutch trading vessel that sank in 1633 during an autumn voyage from Morocco to the Netherlands. According to newly discovered records, the ship encountered "much tempestuous weather" and sprang a leak, sinking near Salcombe. The entire crew survived and salvaged most of the cargo, including 150 bags of gum arabic, 64 bags of saltpetre, 320 goat skins, and 9,000 Barbary ducats (gold Moroccan coins). However, over 400 coins remained on the seabed until 1995.

The coins, now displayed at the British Museum, are pure West African gold stamped into Moroccan ducats. Dave Parham, professor of maritime archaeology at Bournemouth University, noted that the discovery provides "tangible evidence of the flourishing 17th-century maritime trade linking Morocco, the Low Countries, and Britain." The Dutch often melted down African gold to create their own coins, which were a prominent trade currency. The wreck site also yielded everyday items like resin-coated pills, faba beans, pottery, and a stamp seal, offering a glimpse into life aboard the vessel. Jeremy Hill, head of research at the British Museum, called it "a discovery of international importance."
why_it_matters: This find shows how pieces of the past can suddenly reshape our understanding of global connections — the coins from Africa turned into Dutch money were part of a web that still influences trade today. For young people, it’s a reminder that history is not just in textbooks but sometimes hidden under the sea, waiting to change the story.

background_read: The 17th century was the Dutch Golden Age, when the Netherlands became one of the world's great sea-trading powers, with ships sailing across the Atlantic, Indian Ocean, and Mediterranean.
The Dom van Keulen was a typical Dutch trading vessel, carrying goods like gum arabic (used in foods and paints) and saltpetre (for gunpowder) from Morocco to the Low Countries.
The Barbary Coast of North Africa — including Morocco — was a key trading partner, minting gold coins called Barbary ducats from West African gold that reached the region via trans-Saharan caravans.
Maritime archaeologists like Dave Parham (a professor at Bournemouth University in England) study shipwrecks to uncover tangible proof of these ancient trade routes.
Many shipwrecks from this period remain undocumented; the 1995 discovery off Salcombe (a town in Devon, England) only recently found its story in historical archives.

perspectives.description: The identification of the Dom van Keulen fills a gap in our knowledge of 17th-century Atlantic trade. It proves how Dutch merchants integrated African gold into Europe's economy, and the well-preserved personal items offer a rare human dimension to maritime history.

The coins were found by divers in 1995 but only recently identified — in that time, the wreck site may have been disturbed by treasure hunters or natural erosion. Underwater heritage is fragile, and slow research can mean looting or damage before full documentation.

The mix of African gold with European trade goods reflects a broader pattern of bullion moving across continents to finance expanding empires. The fact that the Dutch melted African gold into their own coinage underscores how currency systems were already globalizing long before the modern era.

Now that the coins are at the British Museum, scholars can study the metal purity and stamp marks to trace their exact African origin. Future dives might reveal more of the Dom van Keulen’s structure, offering a clearer picture of shipbuilding and daily life aboard a 17th-century trader.
